title: Trauma craniotomy for extradural haematoma
subtitle: With decompressive craniectomy as the bailout

sources.title: Guidelines for the surgical management of traumatic brain injury (Bullock et al, Neurosurgery 2006;58(3 Suppl):S2-1 to S2-62)
Guidelines for the management of severe traumatic brain injury, 4th edition
Trial of decompressive craniectomy for traumatic intracranial hypertension (Hutchinson et al, N Engl J Med 2016;375:1119-30)

indications: Extradural haematoma over 30 cm3, regardless of GCS.
Extradural haematoma in a comatose patient with anisocoria, as soon as possible.
Smaller extradural haematoma with neurological deterioration or a focal deficit.
Decompressive craniectomy: brain swelling at the end of evacuation that prevents safe bone flap replacement, or, separately, as a last-tier option for refractory raised ICP.
contraindications: Small extradural haematoma in a GCS above 8 without focal deficit, meeting criteria for observation in a neurosurgical centre.
Unsurvivable injury, where operating changes nothing; this is a senior, documented decision.
Uncorrected coagulopathy is a reason to correct urgently in parallel, not to delay a deteriorating patient.
preparation: Fresh GCS and pupils; most recent CT open in theatre.
Blood cross-matched; coagulopathy correction started; tranexamic acid and blood products per the trauma protocol.
Shave and mark the flap before draping; prepare a wide field in case a craniectomy is needed.
Consent from family where possible, but do not delay an emergency evacuation for it.
positioning: Supine, shoulder roll on the side of the haematoma, head turned to the opposite side.
Head on a horseshoe or in pins per the surgeon's choice; pins add time in an emergency.
Reverse Trendelenburg to reduce venous pressure, maintaining cerebral perfusion pressure.
equipment: High-speed drill with perforator and craniotome footplate.
Bipolar diathermy, bone wax, haemostatic agents, dural hitch sutures.
Dural substitute or pericranium for duraplasty.
Means to store a bone flap per local policy (bone bank or abdominal subcutaneous pocket).
anatomy: Most extradural haematomas are temporal or temporoparietal, from a fracture tearing the middle meningeal artery or its branches.
The pterion is where the frontal, parietal, temporal and sphenoid bones meet; the anterior branch of the middle meningeal artery runs beneath it.
The haematoma strips the dura from the inner table. The brain beneath is often normal, which is why the outcome after early surgery is good.
For a decompressive craniectomy, the flap must reach the floor of the middle cranial fossa, or the temporal lobe still herniates against the tentorium.
criticalSafety: Confirm the side from the scan in theatre. A unilateral fixed pupil usually, but not always, points to the side of the clot.
Get to the clot fast: the first burr hole over the thickest part of the haematoma decompresses before the flap is raised.
Find and control the bleeding source before closing. An uncontrolled middle meningeal artery re-accumulates within hours.
If the brain swells beyond the bone edge, leave the bone out rather than force it back.
structuresAtRisk: Middle meningeal artery and foramen spinosum
Superior sagittal sinus and transverse sinus near flap margins
Frontal branch of the facial nerve and superficial temporal artery
Frontal air sinus in an anterior flap
commonErrors: A flap that is too small, leaving clot under the bone edge and making bleeding control impossible.
Not hitching the dura, allowing a fresh extradural to form under the replaced flap.
Missing a contralateral or subdural haematoma that appears once the tamponade of the first clot is released.
Replacing the bone over a swelling brain.
complications: Recurrent extradural or new subdural, intracerebral or contralateral haematoma.
After craniectomy: hydrocephalus, subdural hygroma, syndrome of the trephined, and the need for a later cranioplasty.
Death or severe disability, particularly when surgery is delayed.
postop: Intensive care for intubated patients with ICP monitoring as indicated.
Post-operative CT per local protocol, and at once for any deterioration.
Record where the bone flap is stored and label the head wound and notes 'no bone flap' after a craniectomy.
Plan cranioplasty timing and helmet use after craniectomy.

steps.emphasis: In an emergency, document the best-interests decision; do not delay for a signature.
Pupils and motor score immediately before induction, and the scan read aloud for the side.
Shoulder roll and head turned so the haematoma is uppermost; keep the jugular veins free.
Mark a trauma question-mark incision that can be extended to a full decompressive flap if needed.
First burr hole over the thickest clot: this alone relieves pressure in a herniating patient.
Open the dura only if it is blue, tense, or the scan shows a subdural component.
After a craniectomy, use a loose duraplasty so the swelling brain has room.
State whether the bone flap is replaced or stored, and where.

step.edh.scalp-flap.title: Scalp flap
step.edh.scalp-flap.why: The scalp is very vascular and blood loss from the edges is significant in a coagulopathic trauma patient. A well-planned flap with a broad base also heals reliably.
how: Incise down to bone, staying about 1 cm in front of the tragus to protect the superficial temporal artery and the frontal branch of the facial nerve.
Control the edges with scalp clips or haemostats as you go.
Reflect the scalp with or without the temporalis muscle, depending on the exposure needed.
structuresAtRisk: Frontal branch of the facial nerve
pitfalls: Losing significant blood from the scalp edges before the bone is even opened.

step.edh.bone-flap.title: Raising the bone flap
step.edh.bone-flap.why: The flap must expose the whole clot and its bleeding source. Too small a flap leaves clot under the bone edge and the bleeding vessel out of reach.
how: Connect burr holes with the craniotome footplate, separating the dura from the inner table first.
Lift the bone flap off carefully; the clot is often adherent to it.
Rongeur the temporal bone down towards the middle fossa floor if the clot extends there.
structuresAtRisk: Venous sinuses at the flap margins
pitfalls: Crossing a venous sinus with the craniotome.

step.edh.evacuate.title: Evacuating the clot and controlling the source
step.edh.evacuate.why: Removing the clot relieves compression; finding the bleeding vessel prevents re-accumulation. Both are needed.
how: Remove the clot with suction and irrigation, without pressing on the dura.
Find the bleeding point: usually a branch of the middle meningeal artery, occasionally a sinus or diploic bleeding.
Coagulate the artery; if it bleeds from the foramen spinosum, pack it with bone wax or a haemostatic agent.
Place circumferential dural hitch sutures to the bone edge to close the extradural space.
pitfalls: Closing without identifying the source because bleeding has temporarily stopped under a lower blood pressure.

step.edh.decompressive-craniectomy.title: Bailout: decompressive craniectomy
step.edh.decompressive-craniectomy.why: If the brain swells beyond the bone edge, replacing the flap converts a decompression into a compression. Leaving the bone out saves life, accepting more survivors with disability.
how: Recognise the indication: brain bulging above the inner table, or a tense dura that does not relax after clot removal.
Enlarge the bone opening to a large frontotemporoparietal craniectomy, reaching down to the middle fossa floor.
Open the dura widely and perform a loose duraplasty with pericranium or a substitute.
Do not replace the bone flap. Store it per local policy and record where it is.
Tell the anaesthetist and intensive care team this has been done, and discuss the prognosis honestly with the family.
structuresAtRisk: Temporal lobe herniating through a small defect
Cortical veins at the bone edge
pitfalls: A small craniectomy, which allows the brain to herniate through the bone edge and infarct.
Not recording that the flap is out, so the patient is later turned onto the unprotected side.

step.edh.flap-replace.title: Replacing the bone flap
step.edh.flap-replace.why: Secure bone fixation restores cranial protection and contour; a central hitch stitch prevents a new extradural forming under the flap.
how: Replace the flap only if the brain is slack and below the inner table.
Place a central dural hitch through the flap before fixing it.
Fix with plates and screws or other cranial fixation per local practice.
structuresAtRisk: Dura and cortex under the fixation points
pitfalls: Forcing the bone back over a brain that is beginning to swell.
